title: Friday afternoon
hookLine: shopping, cooking and cleaning done early, so Shabbat can arrive calmly
tomorrow: Abraham left God mid-conversation to run to strangers. rude, or right?

cards: Meal-prep videos make Sunday look serene: containers lined up, everything labeled, the week handled before it starts. The Talmud has its own version, for Fridays, and it's surprisingly hands-on.
It names sages who had students and helpers, and still did the Shabbat preparations themselves. Rav Safra singed the head of the animal for the meal. Rava salted the fish.
So why would a respected teacher do the kitchen work himself?

teach.b: The Talmud's answer is a principle: a mitzvah you do yourself is greater than one done through someone else. And it gives these very sages as the example.
Getting ready for Shabbat is part of honoring it, so they wanted their own hands in it.

teach.h: TOIL ON THE EVE, EAT ON SHABBAT.
teach.b: A second teaching makes it practical: whoever toils on the eve of Shabbat eats on Shabbat. In traditional practice nothing is cooked once the day begins, so tomorrow's rest is built today, hour by hour.
That eve has its own name: erev Shabbat. Then a third sage shows what all the work is for.

teach.h: GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.
teach.b: As the sun went down, Rabbi Hanina would wrap himself in his cloak and say: come, let's go out to greet the Shabbat queen. You can't go out to greet a queen while you're still scrubbing a pot by the door.
That's ready before sunset. Not perfection; a calm arrival.
The shopping, the cooking and the cleaning get pulled earlier, to Thursday if possible, so that when sunset comes there's nothing left to do but walk out to meet it.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, a sage salted the Shabbat fish himself, on purpose.

how: In observant homes Friday is erev Shabbat: food is cooked, the house cleaned, the table set and showers taken before sunset, and some families do much of the cooking on Thursday. Candle-lighting times are published for each town, a short while before sunset.

o: the last workday before the weekend's errands
a quick nap taken before the evening meal
the hours of getting ready before Shabbat begins

games.q: friday, in the Talmud — tap the pairs.
p: went out to greet the Shabbat queen

s: the sages left Shabbat preparations to their students and helpers
the Talmud names sages who did it themselves: one salted fish, one singed a head.
a teaching says a mitzvah done yourself is greater than one done through someone else
Kiddushin 41a, with these very sages as the example.
rushing in at the last minute shows how much you care about Shabbat
the work is pulled earlier so you can go out and greet Shabbat calmly.

games.q: your sister's hosting her in-laws for a holiday dinner Saturday and plans to 'just do it all Saturday morning.' what would Friday afternoon's teaching suggest?
o: do it all at once; last-minute energy makes a better meal.
pull one or two tasks earlier, so she can greet them calmly at the door.
hire it all out; doing the work herself doesn't add anything.
games.why: toil on the eve, eat on the day; and a mitzvah done yourself counts more. early prep is what makes a calm arrival possible.

practice: Name one Friday task you could move earlier: the shopping, one dish, setting the table. Choose the exact moment you'll do it, Wednesday after work or Thursday before bed, and say the plan to yourself in one sentence.
Then let yourself see Friday at sunset with that one thing already done.

wordCard.voice: Friday afternoon: erev Shabbat, the hours of getting ready, done early and with your own hands, so Shabbat can arrive calmly.

orig.note: Hebrew: the eve of Shabbat, Friday's time of getting ready.

carryVoice: The line for this week: ready before sunset. Done early, so you can go out and greet it.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119a (sages who prepared for Shabbat themselves; Rabbi Hanina greets the Shabbat queen)
Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 41a (a mitzvah done oneself is greater than through an agent; Rav Safra and Rava as examples)
Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 3a (who toils on the eve of Shabbat eats on Shabbat)
